assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evidence on how import competition and technology reshape labour demand, local labour markets and wage inequality changed both academic and policy debate. Its identification strategy and local-labour-market framing have been widely adopted.
assessment.attribution: The China-shock empirical programme is clearly credited to Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Katz is a major figure in the wider technology and inequality literature, but the three-name team is the tightest credit for the trade-shock work, and the task-based framework has other originators not on this ballot.
assessment.maturity: The work has had about a decade of replication, extension and critical re-examination, including debates over magnitudes and persistence. It is mature enough for recognition.
uncertainties: Some of the task-based framework's credit lies with people outside this ballot entry.
Debate continues over the long-run persistence of the trade-shock effects and over how much to attribute to trade versus technology.
The committee may prefer a broader labour-and-technology prize.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting reorganised international trade theory and empirics. The framework introduced new channels for gains from trade and is now standard in quantitative trade and in macro and growth models with firm dynamics.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the central contribution, and Helpman is a leading developer of the wider firm-level and heterogeneous-firm trade research. Redding has important quantitative and spatial extensions but the core credit is clearer for the two chosen names. Other contributors outside the ballot, such as Bernard and Eaton–Kortum, complicate the attribution.
assessment.maturity: More than twenty years of use, with a deep empirical literature and policy relevance. The timing is ripe.
uncertainties: Credit may be split with other firm-level trade scholars not listed here.
The committee may prefer a trade prize organised differently, for instance around quantitative trade models.
Helpman has other major contributions, which may complicate how the citation is framed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Partial identification changed how econometricians and applied researchers think about what data can credibly reveal, replacing point-identification assumptions with bounds and set inference. The work is conceptually foundational and has applications in many fields.
assessment.attribution: Manski is the clear originator of the bounds approach. Tamer is central to the moment-inequality and incomplete-models econometrics, and Molinari to inference on identified sets. A two-name award is cleanest, though a three-name award would be defensible.
assessment.maturity: Manski's work dates from the 1980s and 1990s, and the inference theory was developed over the following decades. The approach has long-run influence, though applied adoption is uneven.
uncertainties: Applied use is narrower than the conceptual importance suggests.
Credit for the inference side is spread over many econometricians beyond the ballot entry.
The committee may judge the econometric-theory case against the broader credibility-revolution awards of 2019, 2021 and similar.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Linking the elasticity of taxable income to optimal tax formulas in sufficient-statistics form made empirical tax policy design tractable and shaped the policy debate on top tax rates.
assessment.attribution: Saez is the central bridge between theory and evidence, and Slemrod is a pioneer of the taxable-income and tax-avoidance literature. Chetty and Stantcheva are also influential, but their strongest credit lies in other work, partly listed under other ballot entries. Saez also appears in B017.
assessment.maturity: The work spans roughly three decades, with extensive replication and cross-country evidence. It is mature.
uncertainties: Saez appears in more than one ballot entry, so the committee would need to decide how to frame a citation.
The empirical elasticity estimates remain contested.
Credit overlaps with the public-economics tradition of Feldstein and others not on the ballot.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework with nominal rigidities is the workhorse of monetary policy analysis in central banks. Its normative and practical influence on how policy is designed and communicated is very large.
assessment.attribution: The ballot lists eight names, so any award must limit the number of people. Woodford (integrated framework and optimal policy), Gali (the canonical model and its empirics) and Taylor (policy rules) are a plausible three, but Calvo, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Gertler and Smets all have real claims and the selection is contestable.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature after 25 or more years, though the 2008 crisis and the post-pandemic inflation have prompted critical reassessment.
uncertainties: The three-name cap means a hard and contestable cut among eight credible contributors.
Parts of the framework were challenged by the financial crisis and the 2021–23 inflation.
Earlier laureates (Lucas, Prescott, Kydland, Sargent, Sims) already covered adjacent areas.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Reviving monopsony as an empirical framework for labour markets reshaped debates on minimum wages, wage-setting and inequality. It is a substantive rethinking of the competitive benchmark.
assessment.attribution: Manning's book and its empirical programme are the central contribution. Ashenfelter has important work on minimum wages and labour demand but is more tangential to the monopsony claim, and Naidu has important but more recent work. Card and Krueger on minimum wages were already recognised in 2021, which overlaps.
assessment.maturity: The conceptual line is more than twenty years old, and the empirical evidence on labour-market power has grown considerably in recent years. Some elements remain unsettled.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2021 prize for the labour-market natural-experiment tradition.
A single-laureate award is uncommon.
The empirical estimates of labour-market power are still debated.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Machine-learning methods for causal inference and heterogeneous treatment effects, including causal forests and double/debiased ML, have expanded the toolkit for applied researchers and are widely used inside and outside economics.
assessment.attribution: Athey, Wager and Chernozhukov are strongly associated with the core methods, but credit is shared with statisticians and other economists who are not on the ballot. Athey and Chernozhukov also appear in other ballot entries.
assessment.maturity: The work is only about a decade old. Adoption is rapid, but the long-run durability and the final shape of the methods are not yet known.
uncertainties: The field is young, so the committee may prefer to wait.
Credit overlaps with statistics and computer science.
Whether the methods change substantive economic knowledge, as opposed to practice, remains open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Linking resource misallocation across firms to aggregate TFP and cross-country income differences gave growth and development economists a measurable mechanism and a shared quantitative framework with substantial policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Hsieh and Klenow (2009) is the central paper, with Restuccia and Rogerson (2008) also foundational. The ballot lists Restuccia rather than Rogerson, so credit for the origin of the framework is arguably incomplete. I disclose a conflict: I am a long-time co-author of Klenow, and the committee should weigh this ranking accordingly.
assessment.maturity: Fifteen years or more of use, though the measurement of misallocation, such as markups versus distortions and measurement error, remains actively debated.
uncertainties: Personal conflict through collaboration with Klenow. I disclose it without adjudicating it.
The ballot omits Richard Rogerson, which makes the attribution questionable.
Measurement challenges to the misallocation estimates.
The 2024 and 2025 prizes already covered growth and institutions, which may reduce the committee's appetite.
